links.note: In 1847 the Patriarch of Antioch condemned Mathew Mar Athanasius, the reforming bishop in Kerala. He ordered that 'none shall pray with him'. A rival bishop came from Antioch to check the reform. Then a royal court verdict in 1889 left the two sides as separate churches.

prose_changes.old: These churches descend from Pietist, Moravian, Methodist and Catholic mission lines, and they became the parents of the Christian traditions now flourishing across the global South. Converts also became missionaries in their own right — Lott Carey's mission to Liberia in 1821, sent by Black American churches, is one example.
prose_changes.new: These churches grew out of Protestant mission societies. The societies learned from earlier Pietist, Moravian and Methodist missions. In 1792 William Carey wrote the appeal that led to the Baptist mission in India. In it he held up the Moravians and the Methodists as models. The churches the societies planted became parents of the faith that now grows fast across the global South. Their own converts soon went out to spread it too. Teachers from Polynesia carried it from island to island.
prose_changes.reason: 'Descend from ... Catholic mission lines' is removed: the four wings named here are Protestant mission churches, and the one vendored text, Carey's Enquiry, cites Catholic missionaries only as proof the work was possible, not as a line of descent. The Moravian and Methodist claims are kept and now carried by Documented links from Carey's Enquiry. 'Pietist' is kept; era 8 owns that link. The Lott Carey example is removed: he was sent from America to Liberia, outside this entry's four regions, the Black Church entry does not name him, and no vendored or repo-cited source supports the sentence. The example is replaced by the Polynesian teachers, already in the description and why. Whole field rewritten.

prose_changes.old: Much of the Christianity of Africa, Asia and the Pacific descends from these churches, and the global South is now the numerical center of the faith: the Anglican Church of Nigeria, the churches of South India, the Pacific island churches and the Chinese church all run back through this window. The translation work left a second legacy nobody planned. Hundreds of languages given a written form, a grammar and a printed literature for the first time, which preserved them as much as it preserved anything doctrinal. And the treatment of Crowther in his last years became a lesson African Christians drew directly. It is one of the roots of the independent African church movements of the following century.
prose_changes.new: Much of the Christianity of Africa, Asia and the Pacific comes from these churches. The global South is now the faith's center by numbers. The Anglican Church of Nigeria, the churches of South India, the Pacific island churches and the Chinese church all trace their roots to these years. The translation work left a second legacy nobody planned. Hundreds of languages got a written form, a grammar and printed books for the first time. That kept them alive as much as it kept any teaching alive. And the way Crowther was treated in his last years became a lesson African Christians learned well. It is one of the roots of the independent African churches of the next century.
prose_changes.reason: 'All run back through this window' is map-layout language; rewritten as 'trace their roots to these years'. prose_changes.old: Known by its watchword, "the evangelization of the world in this generation." The 1910 World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh was its summit, and it became the parent of both the modern ecumenical movement and the independent evangelical missionary agencies that followed. It continued seamlessly into the International Missionary Council, founded in October 1921.
prose_changes.new: Known by its watchword, "the evangelization of the world in this generation." Its high point came at Edinburgh in 1910, at a great world meeting on mission. Two later movements claim that meeting as their root. One is the modern ecumenical movement, which works to bring churches together. The other is the wide world of evangelical mission groups that came later. A committee set up at Edinburgh kept its work going. In October 1921 it handed that work to a new body, the International Missionary Council.
prose_changes.reason: 'It continued seamlessly into the International Missionary Council' says the Student Volunteer Movement itself became the council. The entry's own legacy, and the ecumenical entry, say Edinburgh's continuation committee did, while the SVM went on by itself and faded by mid-century. 'Parent of both ... and the independent evangelical missionary agencies' is softened to the claim of ancestry the legacy already makes. Stanley 2009 (repo-cited) for both; the ecumenical claim is carried by a Dominant Modern Reconstruction link.

prose_changes.old: Edinburgh's continuation committee became the International Missionary Council in 1921 and fed into the World Council of Churches in 1948: the modern ecumenical movement dates its own beginning to that room. The same generation's evangelistic energy went the other way, into the independent missionary agencies that multiplied through the twentieth century, so that one gathering is claimed as an ancestor by two movements that spent the following century largely apart. The Student Volunteer Movement itself never recovered from the First World War and had effectively ended by mid-century.
prose_changes.new: The committee set up at Edinburgh became the International Missionary Council in 1921. In 1961 the council joined the World Council of Churches. The modern ecumenical movement dates its own start to that room in Edinburgh. The same generation's zeal for preaching also went the other way. It went into the independent mission groups that grew all through the twentieth century. So two movements that spent the next hundred years mostly apart both claim one meeting as their root. The Student Volunteer Movement itself never got over the First World War. By the middle of the century it had in effect come to an end.
prose_changes.reason: 'Fed into the World Council of Churches in 1948' reads as the missionary council joining at the council's founding. The ecumenical entry's own text says the International Missionary Council merged in at New Delhi in 1961; the field now says so. The rest is reworded into shorter sentences to meet the reading target; no fact is added or dropped.

prose_changes.old: Indonesia now has one of the largest Christian populations of any Muslim-majority country in the world, numbering in the tens of millions, and the Batak church founded in this window counts several million members on its own. A fact that would surprise most people's mental map of where Lutherans live. The universities, schools and hospitals that grew out of the mission remain, one of them carrying Nommensen's name. The great Timor revival of 1965 to 1971, one of the largest recorded in the twentieth century, belongs to the next chapter of the same story.

prose_changes.old: The Mar Thoma Church is an ancient-rite church that added evangelical reform, continuing the St. Thomas Christian tradition of Kerala. After the 1889 court verdict split the community, the larger Malankara Orthodox (Jacobite) body carried on as a separate tradition. Independent revivals in the Khasi, Mizo and Naga hills, meanwhile, made those regions among the most thoroughly Christian on earth.
prose_changes.new: The Mar Thoma Church is an ancient-rite church that added evangelical reform. It carries on the St. Thomas Christian tradition of Kerala. The reform split the community. In 1847 the Patriarch of Antioch condemned its leading bishop. After a royal court verdict in 1889, the larger body, loyal to Antioch, went on as a separate church. Meanwhile, in the Khasi, Mizo and Naga hills, independent revivals made those regions among the most Christian on earth.
prose_changes.reason: 'The larger Malankara Orthodox (Jacobite) body' names a division that came only in 1912, when that body itself split into Orthodox and Jacobite wings. The field now names the body by its loyalty to Antioch and adds the 1847 anathema, which the vendored patriarchal letter documents (Philipos, ed. Howard 1869). The 1889 verdict rests on Frykenberg and the entry's own description. 'Continuing the St. Thomas Christian tradition' is kept; eras 6 and 7 own that link. The rest is split into shorter sentences for the reading target.
